newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl breaks ground for new German chancellery.
newsitem.headline: Kohl breaks ground for new German chancellery.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Tuesday Germany's new chancellery building near the Reichstag in Berlin will be a modest structure and reflect "a relaxed self-confident" nation in the next century.

Speaking at a groundbreaking ceremony for the new chancellery, Kohl said the boxy modern structure would stand in an area that has seen all the "splendour and hubris, destruction and recommencement" of recent German history.

The 400-million mark ($240 million) complex, which is the last major building project in the construction crane-filled capital, may not be finished by the time the government moves to Berlin from Bonn in 1999.

"The building will be modest," Kohl told 200 dignitaries on hand for the government's first formal groundbreaking ceremony in Berlin. "At the end of this century, which has given us so many chances, we Germans have all the reason to be modest now."

Kohl lifted three scoops of dirt from the ground, which had to be softened up by workers for the 30-minute ceremony, held amid bulldozers and construction equipment, because freezing temperatures and biting winds had hardened the ground.
The ceremony took place in a tree-lined field 500 metres (yards) west of the Reichstag, gutted by construction workers racing to renovate the building before 1999.

"We hope for a good and peaceful future here," Kohl said, speaking of the terrain had seen fierce fighting in the closing days of World War Two. "In 1945 this area was in ruins. We hope that ruins will never again result from German polices."
The new H-shaped chancellery will overlook a bend in the Spree River and will have a clear view of the Reichstag.

It will be Berlin's third chancellery in this century. Until the 1930s, chancellors used Bismarck's offices in the nearby Wilhelmstrasse, close to where Hitler built his New Reich Chancellery that was destroyed in World War Two.
"The design radiates a relaxed self-confidence," Kohl said in his speech. "It unites modesty with dignity."
Kohl said united Germany was already becoming an important stopover point for world leaders and that trend would continue.
"We can already see in Bonn that Germany is one of the most visited places (for world leaders)," Kohl said. "It is one of the two or three world capitals with the most official visits."
Pointing towards the Reichstag, Germany's first and future parliament building, Kohl said: "The Reichstag was built under the Kaisers. It stands for democracy.
"It was destroyed after the end of the Weimar Republic, as democracy itself was destroyed. Its reconstruction after the war stood for the new beginning of a democratic state."

The groundbreaking for the chancellery marked a symbolic point-of-no-return for the government's move from the former western capital of Bonn. Parliament voted in 1991 to move to Berlin but planning feuds brought long delays.
"It is now clear that all the talk about deadlines will now be confined to the history books," said Berlin Mayor Eberhard Diepgen. "The decision is made, the deadlines will be met."
Renovation work is underway in the former East German ministry buildings which will house their all-German equivalents from 1999.

Not wanting to hold up the move, Kohl has agreed the State Council Building -- former seat of East Germany's collective presidency under Erich Honecker -- should be used as a temporary chancellery if the new building is not ready on time.
The new chancellery will be ecologically correct with solar panels to generate some of its energy. It will have 310 offices and 13 winter gardens.
Only a short stroll away from the Reichstag will stand one of three new office complexes for parliamentarians.
The upper house of parliament will move into the Prussian Landtag, a classical building just off the central Potsdamer Platz square that was split by the Berlin Wall.
